claim: The capacity of cortical circuits to undergo plasticity in response to experience is a fundamental feature of the brain.
source: The capacity of cortical circuits to undergo plasticity in response to experience is a fundamental feature of the brain (Buonomano and Merzenich, 1998; Costandi, 2016; Li, 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Cortical plasticity can be induced by active, task-dependent training, such as visual perceptual learning.
source: This plasticity can be induced not only by active, task-dependent training, such as visual perceptual learning (Watanabe and Sasaki, 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Lu and Dosher, 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on visual perceptual learning

claim: Cortical plasticity can be induced by passive, repetitive exposure.
source: This plasticity can be induced not only by active, task-dependent training, such as visual perceptual learning (Watanabe and Sasaki, 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Lu and Dosher, 2022), but also by passive, repetitive exposure (Gutnisky et al., 2009; Sasaki et al., 2010; Ekman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on passive exposure

claim: After repeated exposure to a moving dot sequence, flashing a dot at the starting point of the sequence elicits successive elevated neural responses in visual cortex in humans.
source: For instance, after repeated exposure to a moving dot sequence, flashing a dot (i.e. cue) at the starting point of the sequence elicits successive elevated neural responses in visual cortex, akin to those induced by the actual moving dot sequence in both humans (Ekman et al., 2017; Ekman et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior human studies

claim: After repeated exposure to a moving dot sequence, flashing a dot at the starting point of the sequence elicits successive elevated neural responses in visual cortex in animals.
source: For instance, after repeated exposure to a moving dot sequence, flashing a dot (i.e. cue) at the starting point of the sequence elicits successive elevated neural responses in visual cortex, akin to those induced by the actual moving dot sequence in both humans (Ekman et al., 2017; Ekman et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2021) and animals (Eagleman and Dragoi, 2012; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior animal studies

claim: Cue-triggered reactivation is thought to be driven by expectations and is prediction-related.
source: This cue-triggered reactivation is thought to be driven by expectations and is prediction-related (Ekman et al., 2017; Ekman et al., 2023)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Cue-triggered reactivation facilitates the prediction of upcoming stimuli and influences the perception of sensory information.
source: This cue-triggered reactivation is thought to be driven by expectations and is prediction-related (Ekman et al., 2017; Ekman et al., 2023), as it facilitates the prediction of upcoming stimuli and influences the perception of sensory information (Gutnisky et al., 2009; Baker et al., 2014; Pojoga et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Expectation sharpens neural tuning and enhances the processing of expected stimuli.
source: This aligns with the view that expectation sharpens neural tuning and enhances the processing of expected stimuli (Kok et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Expectation elevates the pre-stimulus baseline activity of sensory neurons tuned to expected stimuli.
source: For instance, expectation has been shown to elevate the pre-stimulus baseline activity of sensory neurons tuned to expected stimuli (Wyart et al., 2012; Kok et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Expectation preactivates stimulus templates in the visual cortex.
source: expectation has been shown to elevate the pre-stimulus baseline activity of sensory neurons tuned to expected stimuli (Wyart et al., 2012; Kok et al., 2014) and to preactivate stimulus templates in both the visual (Kok et al., 2017) and auditory (Demarchi et al., 2019) cortices.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on visual cortex

claim: Expectation preactivates stimulus templates in the auditory cortex.
source: expectation has been shown to elevate the pre-stimulus baseline activity of sensory neurons tuned to expected stimuli (Wyart et al., 2012; Kok et al., 2014) and to preactivate stimulus templates in both the visual (Kok et al., 2017) and auditory (Demarchi et al., 2019) cortices.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on auditory cortex

claim: Memory consolidation following training with a temporal sequence is associated with replay.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that memory consolidation (Carr et al., 2011; Gridchyn et al., 2020; Gillespie et al., 2021) or learning process Igata et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021b; Liu et al., 2022 following training with a temporal sequence is associated with a neural phenomenon known as replay.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Learning processes following training with a temporal sequence are associated with replay.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that memory consolidation (Carr et al., 2011; Gridchyn et al., 2020; Gillespie et al., 2021) or learning process Igata et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021b; Liu et al., 2022 following training with a temporal sequence is associated with a neural phenomenon known as replay.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Replay refers to the sequential reactivation of neural activity patterns associated with the trained sequence in both sleep and awake states.
source: Replay refers to the sequential reactivation of neural activity patterns associated with the trained sequence in both sleep (Lee and Wilson, 2002) and awake (Foster and Wilson, 2006) states.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: During replay, the neural representation of the trained sequence is temporally compressed.
source: During replay, the neural representation of the trained sequence is temporally compressed and can occur in either a forward or backward direction (Carr et al., 2011; Joo and Frank, 2018; Nour et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022; McFadyen et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: During replay, the neural representation can occur in either a forward or backward direction.
source: During replay, the neural representation of the trained sequence is temporally compressed and can occur in either a forward or backward direction (Carr et al., 2011; Joo and Frank, 2018; Nour et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022; McFadyen et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Replay events frequently coincide with sharp-wave ripples (SWRs), which are high-frequency (150–220 Hz) oscillations.
source: These replay events frequently coincide with sharp-wave ripples (SWRs), which are high-frequency (150–220 Hz) oscillations (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Bush et al., 2022) detected in hippocampal local field potentials (Buzsáki, 1986; Buzsáki, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Sharp-wave ripples are detected in hippocampal local field potentials.
source: These replay events frequently coincide with sharp-wave ripples (SWRs), which are high-frequency (150–220 Hz) oscillations (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Bush et al., 2022) detected in hippocampal local field potentials (Buzsáki, 1986; Buzsáki, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Replay has been observed in tasks involving sequences, such as nonlocal reinforcement learning.
source: To date, replay has been observed in tasks involving sequences, such as nonlocal reinforcement learning (Liu et al., 2021b) and episodic memory retrieval (Wimmer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Replay has been observed in tasks involving sequences, such as episodic memory retrieval.
source: To date, replay has been observed in tasks involving sequences, such as nonlocal reinforcement learning (Liu et al., 2021b) and episodic memory retrieval (Wimmer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: In Experiment 1, participants were exposed to a predefined sequence of four motion directions for about 30 min.
source: In Experiment 1, we included three trial conditions: full sequence trials, start-only trials, and end-only trials (Figure 1A). In a full sequence trial, participants were exposed to a predefined sequence of the four RDKs presented either clockwise (i.e. 0° → 90° → 180° → 270°) or counterclockwise at the center of the screen, with an interstimulus interval of 300 ms between every two RDKs.
evidence: Describes the experimental procedure

claim: The four successive RDKs in the full sequence trials evoked four comparable peaks after stimulus onset.
source: We found that the four successive RDKs in the full sequence trials evoked four comparable peaks after stimulus onset (Figure 1C, inset figure in the left panel; two-tailed t-test; all ts(17) > 6.8072, all ps<10–5).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 1C

claim: In start-only trials, significant peaks were observed during the periods corresponding to the intervals of the second and third RDKs in the full sequence trials.
source: Interestingly, in start- and end-only trials, significant peaks were still observed during the periods corresponding to the intervals of the second and third RDKs in the full sequence trials (Figure 1C, inset figures in the middle and right panels; start-only condition, two-tailed t-test; all ts(17) > 4.5790, all ps<10–3; end-only condition, two-tailed t-test; all ts(17) > 6.0140, all ps <10–4).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 1C

claim: In end-only trials, significant peaks were observed during the periods corresponding to the intervals of the second and third RDKs in the full sequence trials.
source: Interestingly, in start- and end-only trials, significant peaks were still observed during the periods corresponding to the intervals of the second and third RDKs in the full sequence trials (Figure 1C, inset figures in the middle and right panels; start-only condition, two-tailed t-test; all ts(17) > 4.5790, all ps<10–3; end-only condition, two-tailed t-test; all ts(17) > 6.0140, all ps <10–4).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 1C

claim: No significant peak was observed during the period corresponding to the interval of the last RDK in start-only trials.
source: However, no significant peak was observed during the period corresponding to the interval of the last RDK (start-only condition, two-tailed t-test; t(17) = 1.3221, p=0.2036; end-only condition, two-tailed t-test; t(17) = 0.2473, p=0.8076).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: No significant peak was observed during the period corresponding to the interval of the last RDK in end-only trials.
source: However, no significant peak was observed during the period corresponding to the interval of the last RDK (start-only condition, two-tailed t-test; t(17) = 1.3221, p=0.2036; end-only condition, two-tailed t-test; t(17) = 0.2473, p=0.8076).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Cue-triggered elevated neural responses were observed following visual exposure to the RDK sequences.
source: These results demonstrate cue-triggered elevated neural responses following visual exposure to the RDK sequences, resembling previous studies using simple white dot sequences (Ekman et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2021).
evidence: Inference from experimental results and comparison to prior research

claim: At the group level, decoding accuracies peaked at 411 ms, 464ms, 444 ms, and 434 ms after stimulus onset for motion directions 0°, 90°, 180°, and 270°, respectively.
source: At the group level, decoding accuracies peaked at 411 ms, 464ms, 444 ms, and 434 ms after stimulus onset for motion directions 0° (55.37%±1.21), 90° (58.10%±1.14), 180° (54.07%±1.47), and 270° (53.64%±1.34), respectively.
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis of experimental data

claim: There were no significant differences among the four motion directions in terms of latency at the peak time point.
source: There were no significant differences among the four motion directions in terms of either latency (F(3, 51)=0.375, p=0.7716, ηp2=0.0159) or decoding accuracy (F(3, 51)=2.757, p=0.0517, ηp2=0.091) at the peak time point.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: There were no significant differences among the four motion directions in terms of decoding accuracy at the peak time point.
source: There were no significant differences among the four motion directions in terms of either latency (F(3, 51)=0.375, p=0.7716, ηp2=0.0159) or decoding accuracy (F(3, 51)=2.757, p=0.0517, ηp2=0.091) at the peak time point.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: In full sequence trials, the motion direction information could be successfully decoded.
source: In full sequence trials, the motion direction information could be successfully decoded, as evidenced by the highest decoding probability during the interval corresponding to the presentation of the respective RDK (Figure 2A and B, left panels).
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis and reference to Figure 2

claim: In start- and end-only trials, the motion direction of the first RDK (i.e. the cue) could be reliably decoded after stimulus onset.
source: In start- and end-only trials, we could also reliably decode the motion direction of the first RDK (i.e. the cue) after stimulus onset (Figure 2A and B, middle and right panels, only the decoding probability of the first RDK surpasses the peak-level significance threshold obtained from a nonparametric permutation test, FWE corrected across time).
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis and reference to Figure 2

claim: Subsequent motion direction information was absent at the group level during the post-cue blank period in start- and end-only trials.
source: Surprisingly, however, subsequent motion direction information was absent at the group level during the post-cue blank period, where the cue-triggered elevated responses were previously observed (i.e. 0.4–2.8 s after stimulus onset).
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis of experimental data

claim: The cue-triggered elevated response induced by visual sequence exposure was not consistently specific to a particular feature across participants and trials.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the cue-triggered elevated response induced by visual sequence exposure was not consistently specific to a particular feature across participants and trials.
evidence: Inference from experimental results

claim: No spatial correlation was found between any two trained classifiers.
source: We did not find any spatial correlation between any two trained classifiers (highest correlation r<0.12, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: In the start-only condition, evidence of backward replay of the exposed motion sequence was found during the post-cue blank period, with a peak transition lag at 28–40 ms.
source: As shown in Figure 4A and B, in the start-only condition, we found evidence of backward replay of the exposed motion sequence (i.e. the replay sequence was 270° → 180° → 90° → 0° when the exposed motion sequence was 0° → 90° → 180° → 270°) during the post-cue blank period, with a peak transition lag at 28–40 ms (maximal effect at 32 ms-lag: β = −0.0202±0.002, p<1/24 ≈ 0.042, peak-level significance threshold derived from a nonparametric permutation test, FWE corrected across lags, Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by TDLM analysis and reference to Figure 4

claim: In the end-only condition, evidence of backward replay was found during the post-cue blank period, with a peak transition lag at 28–36 ms.
source: In the end-only condition, we also found evidence of backward replay during the post-cue blank period, with a peak transition lag at 28–36 ms (maximal effect at 32 ms-lag: β = −0.0145±0.0016, p<1/24 ≈ 0.042, peak-level significance threshold obtained from a nonparametric permutation test, FWE corrected across lags; Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by TDLM analysis and reference to Figure 4

claim: The replayed sequence was approximately 10 times faster than the evoked activity sequence in the full sequence condition.
source: We found that the replayed sequence was approximately 10 times faster than the evoked activity sequence in the full sequence condition.
evidence: Inference from comparison of time lags in experimental data

claim: In start-only trials, the backward replay predominantly appeared within the third stage of the blank period (1.2–1.8 s after the onset of the blank period).
source: In start-only trials, we found that the backward replay predominantly appeared within the third stage of the blank period (1.2–1.8 s after the onset of the blank period, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.0108), but there were no significant sequenceness in the other three stages (first stage, p=0.7112; second stage, p=0.5566; fourth stage, p=0.6791; Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4C

claim: In end-only trials, the backward replay was more likely to occur during the second and third stages of the blank period, although the results approached, but did not reach, significance.
source: In end-only trials, the backward replay was more likely to occur during the second and third stages of the blank period, although the results approached, but did not reach, significance (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, second stage, p=0.0936; third stage, p=0.0642; Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and reference to Figure 4F

claim: Only the backward replay was detected in both start- and end-only conditions when examining all 24 potential sequences.
source: Finally, in a control analysis, we conducted a comprehensive examination of all 24 potential sequences. Only the backward replay was detected in both start- and end-only conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by control analysis and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: In Experiment 2, no evidence of either forward or backward replay was found in the second-only condition.
source: We found no evidence of either forward or backward replay in either condition (Figure 5A; maximal nonsignificant effect at 32 ms-lag: second-only condition, β = −0.0024±0.0014; third-only condition, β = −0.0018±0.0015).
evidence: Supported by TDLM analysis and reference to Figure 5A

claim: In Experiment 2, no evidence of either forward or backward replay was found in the third-only condition.
source: We found no evidence of either forward or backward replay in either condition (Figure 5A; maximal nonsignificant effect at 32 ms-lag: second-only condition, β = −0.0024±0.0014; third-only condition, β = −0.0018±0.0015).
evidence: Supported by TDLM analysis and reference to Figure 5A

claim: In Experiment 3 start-only condition, a numerical trend of backward replay was found at transition lags at 20–40 ms, although it did not reach statistical significance.
source: In the start-only condition, we found a numerical trend of backward replay at transition lags at 20–40 ms, although it did not reach statistical significance (Figure 5B, left panel; maximum effect at 28 ms-lag: β = −0.0139±0.0021).
evidence: Supported by TDLM analysis and reference to Figure 5B

claim: In Experiment 3 end-only condition, the evidence for backward replay just reached the significance level at transition lags at 20–40 ms.
source: In the end-only condition, the evidence for backward replay just reached the significance level at transition lags at 20–40 ms (Figure 5B, right panel; maximal effect at 24 ms-lag: β = −0.0147±0.0019, p<1/24 ≈ 0.042, using the peak-level significance threshold from a nonparametric permutation test, FWE corrected across lags).
evidence: Supported by TDLM analysis and reference to Figure 5B

claim: A transient ripple power increase at 120–180 Hz was found at the onset of replay events, compared to the baseline period of 50–100 ms prior to replay onset.
source: Using the MEG signals recorded from whole-brain sensors, we found a transient ripple power increase at 120–180 Hz at the onset of replay events, compared to the baseline period of 50–100 ms prior to replay onset (Figure 6A; cluster-based permutation test with cluster forming threshold t>3.1 and 5000 permutations).
evidence: Supported by time-frequency analysis and reference to Figure 6A

claim: The power increase at replay onset was localized to sources in bilateral visual cortex.
source: We found that the power increase at replay onset was localized to sources in bilateral visual cortex (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by source localization analysis and reference to Figure 6C

claim: The right MTL, including the hippocampus and amygdala, was associated with power increase prior to the onset of replay events.
source: Moreover, the right MTL, including the hippocampus and amygdala, was associated with power increase prior to the onset of replay events (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by source localization analysis and reference to Figure 6B

claim: Activation in the MTL occurred 30 ms earlier than that in visual cortex.
source: Specifically, activation (i.e. power increase) in the MTL occurred 30 ms earlier than that in visual cortex (p<0.05, corrected, whole-brain nonparametric permutation test).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of source localization data

claim: Peak activation in visual cortex at replay onset was preceded by peak activation in the MTL.
source: Peak activation in visual cortex at replay onset was preceded by peak activation in the MTL (Figure 6D), implying an information flow from the MTL to visual cortex.
evidence: Supported by time course analysis and reference to Figure 6D

claim: Visual sequence exposure induces twofold brain plasticity: time-locked, non-feature-specific elevated responses and non-time-locked, feature-specific backward replay.
source: We found the coexistence of time-locked, non-feature-specific elevated responses and non-time-locked, feature-specific backward replay after visual sequence exposure in human brain.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The feature-specific backward replay occurred in a time-compressed manner.
source: The feature-specific backward replay occurred in a time-compressed manner and could be triggered only by the first or last stimulus of the sequence.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: The feature-specific backward replay could be triggered only by the first or last stimulus of the sequence.
source: The feature-specific backward replay occurred in a time-compressed manner and could be triggered only by the first or last stimulus of the sequence.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Even brief exposure to the sequence could still induce a trend for the backward replay.
source: Interestingly, even brief exposure to the sequence could still induce a trend for the backward replay.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from Experiment 3

claim: MTL activity preceded the ripple power increase in visual cortex at replay onset.
source: Finally, we observed that MTL activity preceded the ripple power increase in visual cortex at replay onset.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: Prediction-related elevated responses in the dynamic temporal context are not feature-specific.
source: First, different from many previous studies showing that expectation-based responses in static contexts are feature-specific (Wyart et al., 2012; Kok et al., 2014; Kok et al., 2017), we show here that prediction-related elevated responses in the dynamic temporal context are not.
evidence: Inference from experimental findings and comparison to prior research

claim: Non-feature-specific elevated response potentially facilitates the general processing of any upcoming stimuli, rather than stimuli with a specific feature.
source: This non-feature-specific elevated response potentially facilitates the general processing of any upcoming stimuli, rather than stimuli with a specific feature.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings

claim: Even brief exposure to a visual sequence is sufficient to induce replay.
source: Second, contrary to the prevailing notion that replay in learning and memory requires lengthy training with a task, our study shows that even brief exposure to a visual sequence is sufficient to induce replay.
evidence: Inference from experimental findings

claim: The replay may play a critical role in memorizing the visual sequence.
source: The replay we unveiled here may play a critical role in memorizing the visual sequence.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings

claim: The non-feature-specific elevated responses could be induced by rhythmic entrainment.
source: Regarding the twofold neural consequences following the visual sequence exposure, the non-feature-specific elevated responses could be induced by rhythmic entrainment.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings

claim: Rhythmic stimulation can entrain neural oscillations, which in turn facilitates predictions about future inputs and enhances the brain's readiness for incoming stimuli.
source: Substantial evidence supports that rhythmic stimulation can entrain neural oscillations, which in turn facilitates predictions about future inputs and enhances the brain's readiness for incoming stimuli (Lakatos et al., 2008; Lakatos et al., 2013; Herrmann et al., 2016; Barne et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Task-irrelevant information could be more effectively decoded when presented at moments close to a highly probable target presentation.
source: For instance, recent findings demonstrate that even task-irrelevant information could be more effectively decoded when presented at moments close to a highly probable target presentation (Auksztulewicz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The rhythmic presentation of the motion sequence may have entrained oscillatory activity in the brain, leading to periodic activation of sensory cortices.
source: In our study, the rhythmic presentation of the motion sequence may have entrained oscillatory activity in the brain, leading to periodic activation of sensory cortices.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings

claim: Rhythmic entrainment likely serves as a possible mechanism supporting the general facilitation of neural processing for any upcoming stimuli, independent of specific stimulus features.
source: This rhythmic entrainment likely serves as a possible mechanism supporting the general facilitation of neural processing for any upcoming stimuli, independent of specific stimulus features.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings

claim: Feature-specific replay may operate through a different mechanism driven by intrinsic neural processes rather than direct external stimuli.
source: In contrast, feature-specific replay may operate through a different mechanism driven by intrinsic neural processes rather than direct external stimuli.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings

claim: Intrinsic activity is not time-locked to stimulus onset, but instead manifests in a spontaneous way.
source: Therefore, this intrinsic activity is not time-locked to stimulus onset, but instead manifests in a spontaneous way.
evidence: Inference from experimental findings

claim: Feature-specific replay may facilitate the integration of fragmented experiences into coherent representations, thereby subserving visual sequence learning and memory.
source: As a result, feature-specific replay may facilitate the integration of fragmented experiences into coherent representations, thereby subserving visual sequence learning and memory.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings

claim: The elevated responses can be implemented through a simple local synaptic mechanism in visual cortex without top-down guidance.
source: Previous animal studies (Xu et al., 2012; Gavornik and Bear, 2014) showed that this process can be implemented through a simple local synaptic mechanism in visual cortex (Xu et al., 2012) without top-down guidance.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior animal studies

claim: No functional relationship was found between activities in V1 and the hippocampus when exposing human participants to a white dot sequence.
source: Moreover, Ekman et al., 2023, recently found no functional relationship between activities in V1 and the hippocampus when exposing human participants to a white dot sequence, further suggesting that the elevated responses may indeed originate in visual cortex.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The replay events are likely initiated by the hippocampus.
source: Different from the elevated responses, the replay events are likely initiated by the hippocampus.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings

claim: The replay entails reorganizing the motion direction sequence in the brain.
source: Instead, the replay entails reorganizing the motion direction sequence in the brain.
evidence: Inference from experimental findings

claim: Active communication between the hippocampus and visual cortex is involved in the occurrence of replay events.
source: Therefore, we propose the involvement of active communication between the hippocampus and visual cortex in the occurrence of replay events, consistent with the view that the hippocampus encodes relationships among stimuli, whereas visual cortex primarily acts as a platform for the manifestation of replay events (Whittington et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculative interpretation of experimental findings and citation to prior research

claim: The hippocampus encodes relationships among stimuli, whereas visual cortex primarily acts as a platform for the manifestation of replay events.
source: Therefore, we propose the involvement of active communication between the hippocampus and visual cortex in the occurrence of replay events, consistent with the view that the hippocampus encodes relationships among stimuli, whereas visual cortex primarily acts as a platform for the manifestation of replay events (Whittington et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: The exchange of information between the hippocampus and neocortex is critical for facilitating replay events through hippocampal-neocortical circuits.
source: Previous studies on memory consolidation considered the exchange of information between these two regions critical for facilitating replay events through hippocampal-neocortical circuits (Buzsáki, 1996; Ji and Wilson, 2007; Carr et al., 2011; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2016; Buch et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Replay events offer a mechanism for transferring recent experience from the hippocampus to the cortex, enabling the encoding of stimulus relationships in the cortex.
source: Functionally, replay events offer a mechanism for transferring recent experience from the hippocampus to the cortex, enabling the encoding of stimulus relationships in the cortex (Marr and Brindley, 1971; Alvarez and Squire, 1994; Redish and Touretzky, 1998; Dimakopoulos et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: A natural behavioral consequence of visual sequence exposure is visual sequence learning.
source: A natural behavioral consequence of visual sequence exposure is visual sequence learning (Baker et al., 2014; Finnie et al., 2021; Ekman et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The hippocampus is involved in encoding relationships among stimuli.
source: First, the hippocampus is involved in encoding relationships among stimuli (Staresina and Davachi, 2009; Turk-Browne et al., 2009; Hsieh et al., 2014; Garvert et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The ability to encode relationships among stimuli drastically decreases when the hippocampus is damaged.
source: in fact, the ability to encode such relationships drastically decreases when the hippocampus is damaged (Chun and Phelps, 1999; Hannula et al., 2006; Konkel et al., 2008; Schapiro et al., 2014; Finnie et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Visual cortical areas act as a 'cognitive blackboard' where task-relevant features are highlighted through feedback connections.
source: Second, visual cortical areas act as a 'cognitive blackboard' where task-relevant features are highlighted through feedback connections (Roelfsema and de Lange, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: There are strong bidirectional connections between the hippocampus and sensory cortices.
source: Third, there are strong bidirectional connections between the hippocampus and sensory cortices (Eichenbaum et al., 2007; Henke, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Sequential reactivations of feature information initially generated in the hippocampus can be quickly and accurately sent back to the sensory cortices.
source: As proposed by the hippocampal-cortical backward projection model (Rolls, 2000), sequential reactivations of feature information initially generated in the hippocampus can be quickly and accurately sent back to the sensory cortices, consistent with the findings of Ji and Wilson, 2007.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Visual sequence plasticity is impaired when the hippocampus is damaged.
source: A recent study also provided direct evidence that visual sequence plasticity is impaired when the hippocampus is damaged (Finnie et al., 2021), supporting the hypothesis of functional feedback information flow.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: When animals stopped at the end of a rewarded pathway, place cells were reactivated in the reverse order of the previously experienced direction.
source: In rodents, a seminal study of replay during the awake state showed that when animals stopped at the end of a rewarded pathway, place cells were reactivated in the reverse order of the previously experienced direction (Foster and Wilson, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Awake replay could occur in either a forward or backward direction relative to behavioral experience.
source: However, a later study revealed that awake replay could occur in either a forward or backward direction relative to behavioral experience (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: In humans, both forward and backward replay directions have been observed in different nonspatial cognitive tasks.
source: Similarly, in humans, both directions have been observed in different nonspatial cognitive tasks (Liu et al., 2019; Wimmer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Forward replay may be associated with planning.
source: Forward replay may be associated with planning (Ólafsdóttir et al., 2015; Gillespie et al., 2021), providing information pertaining to the assessment of future pathways (Diba and Buzsáki, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Backward replay may be more related to experience, as often observed at the end of runs when animals consume a reward.
source: Backward replay may be more related to experience, as often observed at the end of runs when animals consume a reward (Foster and Wilson, 2006; Ambrose et al., 2016).

claim: Both forward and backward replays are modulated by task demands.
